Patent

/PAT-uhnt/ - the stress falls on PAT · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Patent means readily seen; obvious.

The excuse was patent nonsense: the dog could hardly have eaten homework posted online.

Worked Example

Halfway through the talent show's headline act, the singer lowered her microphone to wave at a friend — and the ballad kept pouring out of the speakers at full strength. A hundred phones came up at once. Nobody needed the recording, though; the lip-sync was exposed for every seat in the auditorium simultaneously.

Patent is the exact word for that exposure, because patent means readily seen; obvious — a fact lying so open that no one has to hunt for it. Blatant would add shamelessness, as if she had waved on purpose; patent simply reports the plain view. The word is Latin patere, to lie open — the same openness in the inventor's patent, originally 'letters patent,' documents published open for all to read.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unmistakable: Unmistakable says a thing cannot be misread, however briefly you look — the signature, the smell of smoke. Patent makes the same claim of obviousness in courtroom-and-editorial dress, and it leans accusatory: patent nonsense, a patent lie — obviousness asserted about a false or foolish thing.

blatant: Blatant is obviousness plus shamelessness — the offender flaunts the thing, daring you to object. Patent reports only the plain view: a patent lie lies open for all to see, but the word says nothing about the liar's nerve. Brazenness wants blatant; bare obviousness wants patent.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

veiled: kept partly out of sight on purpose

imperceptible: too faint for anyone to notice at all

Where it sits · how loudly the truth announces itself — evident → patent → glaring

evident vs. patent: Evident is quieter than patent — an evident truth is there for anyone who takes the trouble to look at the facts, while a patent one lies open before anyone looks.

glaring vs. patent: Glaring goes further than patent — a patent error is plain to any eye; a glaring one seems to shout from the page and dares you to miss it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — patent

Root — patent: lying open (Latin patere, to lie open)

Put it together

Put it together: Patent is Latin patere, to lie open, worn whole into English — there is nothing to peel off here. A patent fact lies open to every eye; letters patent were open letters from the crown, published for all to read, and the inventor's patent keeps that name because the invention's workings are laid open in the public record.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin patere, to lie open, left English almost nothing else you would meet outside an anatomy text — no everyday cousin shares the root. What it left instead is this word's own double life: the adjective (a patent lie, lying open to view) and the noun (an inventor's patent, an exclusive right published in open letters). One root, two doors, both open.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / judicial

The adjective patent is courtroom-and-editorial English, and it keeps one collocational groove: patent nonsense, a patent lie, patent absurdity — obviousness asserted about something false or foolish. Blatant adds shamelessness and glaring adds offense; evident stays neutral and mild. Keep the noun distinct: an inventor's patent is an exclusive right to an invention, and only the etymology — things laid open — connects the two.
